item.title: Medical Device Security
item.description:
From 2024 to 2026 I led cybersecurity engagements for more than ten medical device manufacturers at Harbor Labs, serving as the hardware and embedded security lead and owning scope, client relationships, timelines, and deliverables across each product portfolio.

What the work covered

  • Threat modeling and risk assessment: STRIDE threat models, attack surface analyses, architecture diagrams, and attack and mitigation trees that supported successful FDA 510(k) submissions.
  • Penetration testing and vulnerability assessment: 15+ engagements spanning hardware, firmware, and software, including reverse engineering, cryptanalysis, OS and VM assessment, and cloud auditing.
  • Secure SDLC and compliance: secure coding guides that bring cryptography, TLS, encryption, and key management into CI/CD pipelines, plus risk assessments and regulatory documentation aligned with FDA premarket cybersecurity guidance.

Highlights

  • 10+ medical device manufacturers
  • 15+ penetration testing engagements
  • Documentation behind successful FDA 510(k) submissions

item.title: IoT Security & Privacy
item.description:
Connected devices bring security decisions into homes, workplaces, and shared physical spaces. Our research examines who can use these devices, what their sensors and communications reveal, and how to detect and investigate abuse. It spans wearables, smart homes, IoT infrastructure, and resource-constrained devices.

Telematics devices

At Geotab, I am the hardware and firmware subject-matter expert for the security of our telematics devices, the in-vehicle units that connect fleet vehicles to the cloud. I lead security design reviews and risk assessments for new devices and features, and assess the hardware and firmware attack surface, bringing the same hardware and embedded security practice I applied to medical devices.

Wearable authentication: WACA, PACA, and PINTA

WACA continuously verifies the person using a computer from smartwatch motion sensors while they type. The IEEE SPW study and IEEE TMC article develop the sensor-processing, feature-extraction, user-profiling, and classification pipeline. This brings behavioral verification beyond a single login check. The work also led to a continuous-authentication patent.

The related protocols protect the behavioral information used for verification. PACA combines password-authenticated key exchange with private biometric template matching. PINTA combines a password with host and network behavioral profiles, using fuzzy hashing and fully homomorphic encryption to protect those profiles.

WACA funding

The WACA effort was supported by approximately $500,000 in combined NSF SaTC funding, through awards #1718116 to FIU and #1718109 to Florida Atlantic University. Demos and team details are on the WACA project website.

Smart-home privacy and access control

Peek-a-Boo (WiSec 2020) shows how encrypted wireless traffic can reveal device states and household activities. A cascading ML pipeline identifies devices and states, then models activity sequences, using traffic from Wi-Fi, ZigBee, and BLE devices. We also evaluate a defense that generates cover traffic to obscure device behavior.

Kratos (WiSec 2020) addresses homes where several people share several devices. Its policy manager negotiates conflicting access requests and restrictions, supporting more expressive control than a single-owner model. We implemented and evaluated it in real smart-home deployments.

Our later studies examine access control and authentication in shared IoT devices and privacy perceptions across race and ethnicity, adding the perspectives of the people who use these systems.

IoT cryptojacking and infrastructure abuse

Our NDSS 2022 cryptojacking detector uses network-traffic features to identify unauthorized mining across heterogeneous smart-home devices. We compare supervised classifiers and evaluate an SVM-based detector under aggressive and stealthy mining, different device platforms, and partially or fully compromised networks. These experiments test how attacker behavior and deployment conditions affect detection.

The broader cryptojacking systematization organizes attacks and defenses. Our Docker honeypot study examines related infrastructure abuse through forensic observations of host-resource usage and network traffic.

Smart-environment forensics

VERITAS (NDSS 2022) reconstructs activities and suspicious behavior from smart-environment event logs. A first-order Markov model captures transitions between device states to support forensic inference, including policy violations and signs of tampering. The evaluation uses 22 commercial devices and more than 84,000 incidents.

On-device machine learning for intrusion detection

Our IoT intrusion-detection study compares ML training across cloud, edge, and device platforms, and evaluates TinyML inference on microcontrollers. It measures energy, execution time, and detection performance to understand the cost of keeping analysis close to the device. A companion review of on-device ML surveys energy-aware training and inference, including distributed and federated approaches.

Identity and other connected systems

EVOKE supports efficient revocation of verifiable credentials in constrained IoT networks. Our decentralized-identity survey covers the wider identifier and credential ecosystem.

Related work includes IoT-enabled smart lighting, a security and performance assessment of UAV authentication, and jamming and hijacking attacks on micro aerial drones.

item.title: AI Security
item.description:
My work on machine learning and security began in 2017, well before the recent focus on large language models. It covers three connected questions: how learning can detect security threats, how sensitive information can be inferred through learned models, and how to protect models and the data they use. The methods range from linear regression and statistical sequence models to CNNs, LSTMs, and vision transformers.

AI-assisted security tooling

At Geotab, I build AI-assisted tooling that speeds up vulnerability analysis and reduces manual triage. Findings from static analysis, dependency, infrastructure-as-code, and secret scanning arrive in large volumes; the tooling helps prioritize them and move real issues to remediation with engineering teams faster.

Privacy-preserving learning and collaboration

SM-DDP (IEEE PAC 2017) combines secure multiparty computation and differential privacy for linear regression. We implemented the protocol with HElib and evaluated it on census data and a multi-institution healthcare dataset, enabling analysis while protecting participants’ inputs and limiting information disclosed by the result.

Curie (CODASPY 2019) adds policy-governed data exchange to collaborative analysis. Partners specify who may receive which data and under what conditions; negotiated policies govern the secure computation. A healthcare application evaluates the interaction between sharing policies, privacy, and predictive utility. Our homomorphic encryption survey provides the broader cryptographic background for computing on protected data.

Behavioral user authentication

WACA uses smartwatch motion during typing to build behavioral profiles and continuously verify the user. Its learning pipeline includes sensor preprocessing, feature extraction, user-specific profiling, and classification. The initial IEEE SPW paper and journal study examine the practical tradeoff between observation time and authentication error.

PACA and PINTA extend the privacy side of behavioral verification through protected template comparison and encrypted profiles. These cryptographic protocols complement the behavioral analysis by protecting its sensitive inputs. More context is on the IoT Security & Privacy project.

Inferring smart-home activities from encrypted traffic

Peek-a-Boo (WiSec 2020) uses a sequence of learned decisions to infer devices, their states, and user activities from wireless traffic metadata. The pipeline combines supervised device and state classification with a hidden Markov model for activity sequences. This demonstrates how ML can turn encrypted-traffic patterns into a privacy threat, and motivates our cover-traffic defense.

Detecting cryptojacking and IoT intrusions

Our IoT cryptojacking detector (NDSS 2022) learns from packet timing and size features. We compare logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, SVM, and Gaussian Naive Bayes, then evaluate the SVM detector across mining strategies and network conditions. The cryptojacking survey places such detection techniques in the broader attack and defense landscape.

The on-device IoT intrusion-detection study compares logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, decision trees, random forests, Naive Bayes, and neural networks, measuring the costs of training and inference. TinyML experiments examine deployment on microcontrollers, where energy and latency matter alongside accuracy. Our energy-focused review synthesizes on-device learning approaches and their resource tradeoffs.

Learning activity sequences for forensics

VERITAS (NDSS 2022) learns a first-order Markov model from smart-environment events. It uses device-state transitions to infer activities and investigate anomalies, policy violations, and possible tampering. This is a use of probabilistic sequence learning for security investigation.

ML-based ransomware detection

The RøBguard defense (ACM TWEB 2025) applies machine learning to browser ransomware. It hooks the File System Access API and classifies behavior to identify the ransomware activity studied in our RøB work. The evaluation examines detection effectiveness and runtime overhead. The Web Security project connects this detector to the underlying browser attack surface and complementary defenses.

Adversarial malware detection

Our image-based malware study evaluates a CNN operating on binary images alongside MalConv under four functionality-preserving attacks. Image-based classification was more resistant to the tested black-box byte-append attacks, but both approaches remained vulnerable to white-box FGSM attacks. The result highlights the importance of evaluating detectors against an attacker who actively changes the input.

Our WiSec 2022 WebAssembly study examines how code obfuscation can cause an existing ML cryptojacking detector to miss malicious samples. The follow-up work on evasive Wasm continues this line of research. The patented WASMGUARD represents Wasm binaries as image-patch sequences and uses a vision transformer to classify malicious code, including obfuscated samples.

Deep learning for VR side-channel inference

IMMERSPY (NDSS 2025) recovers spoken-digit information from motion-sensor vibrations caused by a VR headset’s speakers. A CNN-LSTM processes spectrogram representations of the signal. The work also uses generative text-to-speech to produce training examples without requiring labeled recordings from the victim. It studies both informed and uninformed victim settings and evaluates a tone-based defense. See the Mobile Security project for the wider XR context.

item.title: Mobile Security
item.description:
Security patches only protect users once they reach the device. This line of work takes a device-centric view of the Android ecosystem: instead of asking which patches Google releases, it asks which patches actually land on a given phone, how quickly, and for how long.

Android security updates

We collected and analyzed more than 360,000 OEM security updates across vendors, models, and regions, measuring support duration, update frequency, and release delay. The study shows large gaps between vendors and between regions for the same device, and quantifies how many known vulnerabilities accumulate once a device leaves support. A follow-up journal study extends the analysis to the global landscape of Android updates.

Funding and recognition

In 2021, Selcuk Uluagac’s research group received a Google ASPIRE Research Award ($112,000) for Android Security and Privacy Research. I co-led the effort with Selcuk Uluagac and Ahmet Aris. See the FIU award announcement.

The work appeared at NDSS 2024 and was presented at FTC PrivacyCon 2024, Panel 6: Mobile Device Security.

VR sensors and learned side channels

IMMERSPY (NDSS 2025) shows how zero-permission motion sensors can expose vibrations from a headset’s speakers. Signal processing produces spectrograms, and a CNN-LSTM classifies spoken digits that can reveal sensitive sequences. We also use synthetic speech generated through text-to-speech to train without labeled victim recordings, and evaluate a tone-based countermeasure.

Our XR security and privacy article places sensor leakage within the broader risks of extended-reality devices. Wearable behavioral authentication is covered in the IoT Security & Privacy project, while the AI Security project brings together the learning methods used across these systems.

item.title: Web Security
item.description:
Modern browser APIs and the Node.js ecosystem give web applications capabilities that used to belong to native software. This work studies what attackers can do with those capabilities, and how to defend against them.

RøB: ransomware over modern web browsers

Using the File System Access API and WebAssembly, we built RøB, a ransomware strain that runs entirely inside the browser and encrypts files in local, cloud-synced, external, and network-shared folders. We evaluated it across operating systems and antivirus products, showed where existing defenses fall short, and proposed three complementary defenses at the browser, file system, and user levels.

RøBguard: learning to detect browser ransomware

Our ACM TWEB follow-up introduces RøBguard, a machine-learning defense that hooks the File System Access API and classifies behavior associated with browser ransomware. We evaluate its detection effectiveness and overhead against the studied attacks. This adds behavioral detection to the browser, file-system, and user-level defenses explored in the original RøB study.

Unrestricted file uploads in Node.js

We built NodeSec, a tool that generates payloads for 13 unrestricted file upload attacks and tests Node.js file upload libraries and real-world CMSs. It uncovered implementation flaws in popular libraries used by millions of applications, leading to 19 CVEs.

Related work

Our browser API analysis examines the security and privacy consequences of expanding browser capabilities. The cryptojacking survey organizes mining attacks and defenses, including browser-based mining. Our WebAssembly obfuscation study and evasive Wasm work examine how malicious code can evade detection. The AI Security project explains the related adversarial ML and vision-transformer research.

item.title: Applied Cryptography
item.description:
Strong cryptographic primitives only help when they can be deployed efficiently and correctly. This work focuses on bringing privacy-preserving cryptography into real systems.

Post-quantum cryptography migration

At Geotab, I lead the cross-team effort on post-quantum cryptography (PQC) readiness: understanding where and how cryptography is used across products and services, and planning the migration to quantum-resistant algorithms.

Homomorphic encryption

Our survey of homomorphic encryption schemes covers the theory and implementations of partially, somewhat, and fully homomorphic encryption, along with their use in privacy-preserving applications.

Privacy-preserving machine learning

We developed SM-DDP, a protocol that combines secure multiparty computation with differential privacy for linear regression, and implemented it with HElib. We evaluated it on census data and 1,400 patient records from seven medical institutions in the International Warfarin Pharmacogenetics Consortium (IWPC) dataset. The full IWPC dataset was contributed by 21 sites in nine countries; our work used a subset for evaluation.

Policy-governed collaborative learning

Curie (CODASPY 2019) addresses the policy constraints that arise when organizations collaborate on sensitive data. Its CPL language lets each participant specify sharing conditions, negotiate an agreement, and enforce that agreement during secure computation. A healthcare application explores the tradeoffs among policy restrictions, privacy, and analytical utility. Together with SM-DDP, this work puts privacy-preserving learning at the center of our research before the recent LLM era.

PACA and PINTA apply related privacy principles to behavioral authentication, protecting biometric comparisons and user profiles. See the IoT Security & Privacy project for those systems and the AI Security project for the wider ML research.

Decentralized identity

EVOKE provides efficient revocation of verifiable credentials in resource-constrained IoT networks. Our decentralized-identity survey examines identifiers, credentials, and their security and privacy properties.

item.title: Exploiting WebAssembly for Evasive Code Execution over Modern Web Browsers
item.description:
Research overview

This work examines WebAssembly as a vehicle for evasive code execution in modern browsers. It belongs to our broader investigation of browser capabilities and malicious-code detection. Related research includes code obfuscation for WebAssembly and learning-based security analysis, connecting the browser attack surface with the problem of detecting code designed to evade security tools.

item.title: Unveiling the Global Landscape of Android Security Updates
item.description:
Research overview

This follow-up to our NDSS Android study analyzes 567,000 security-update records from 2014 to 2024, covering 904 devices from six OEMs across 98 countries. We compare update timing across manufacturers, devices, and regions, examine documented vulnerabilities and OEM compliance with Android security guidelines, and identify gaps in patch availability and support. The expanded dataset provides a broader view of Android’s global update ecosystem.

item.title: Systems and Methods for Detecting Malicious WebAssembly Modules under Source Code Obfuscation
item.description:
Research overview

This patent describes WASMGUARD, a detector for malicious WebAssembly modules, including samples transformed through source-code obfuscation. Its pipeline builds benign and malicious datasets, converts binaries into image representations, and uses a vision transformer for classification. The approach connects browser security with learning-based malware analysis and the challenge of preserving detection under functionality-preserving code changes.

item.title: System and Method for Real-Time Detection of Unrestricted File Upload Vulnerabilities in Node.js Applications
item.description:
Research overview

This patent describes an automated approach to detecting unrestricted file-upload vulnerabilities in Node.js applications. It combines attack-payload generation, authorization handling, upload automation, and validation of the application’s response. The system tests whether protections against malicious filenames, file types, and file contents hold in practice. The related NodeSec paper explains the broader research and evaluation.

item.title: A Survey on Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials
item.description:
Research overview

This survey explains decentralized identifiers and verifiable credentials, their implementations, and their use across digital-identity applications. It covers scenarios beyond individual identity, including cloud, edge, and IoT resources, and reviews relevant initiatives, adoption challenges, and future research directions. It provides background for our EVOKE credential-revocation mechanism, which targets constrained IoT networks.

item.title: Diversity Perspectives on Access Control and Authentication in Shared IoT Devices
item.description:
Research overview

This paper considers diversity perspectives on access control and authentication for IoT devices shared by multiple people. It adds a human perspective to the question of who can use connected devices and under what conditions. The work complements our IoT Security & Privacy research, including the Kratos smart-home access-control system and research on smart-device privacy perceptions.

item.title: Ransomware over Modern Web Browsers: A Novel Strain and a New Defense Mechanism
Speak Up, I'm Listening: Extracting Speech from Zero-Permission VR Sensors
item.description:
Research overview

IMMERSPY infers spoken digits from motion-sensor vibrations caused by a VR headset’s speakers. It combines spectrogram processing with a CNN-LSTM and evaluates scenarios with and without labeled victim data. Generative text-to-speech supplies synthetic training examples. The study also evaluates a tone-based defense against this acoustic side channel.

item.title: Users' Privacy Perceptions in Smart Devices from Race and Ethnicity Perspectives
item.description:
Research overview

This paper examines users’ perceptions of privacy in smart devices from race and ethnicity perspectives. It brings a human perspective to connected-device privacy, complementing our technical work on information leakage and device security. The study is part of our broader IoT Security & Privacy research, which also covers shared-device access control and authentication.

item.title: With Great Power Comes Great Responsibility: Security and Privacy Issues of Modern Browser Application Programming Interfaces
item.description:
Research overview

This article examines the security and privacy consequences of modern browser APIs that expose device capabilities, manage data, and support user interaction. It organizes the API landscape, discusses risks arising from implementation choices and combinations of capabilities, and outlines research directions for improving defenses. The focus is the balance between richer web applications and the larger attack surface they introduce.

item.title: (In)Security of File Uploads in Node.js
item.description:
Research overview

We developed NodeSec to test Node.js applications and file-upload libraries against 13 types of unrestricted file-upload attacks. The study examines weaknesses in filename, file-type, and content handling, including reliance on insecure library behavior. Our responsible disclosures resulted in 19 CVEs. The paper explains the attack coverage, evaluation, root causes, and recommendations for safer upload implementations.

item.title: A Comprehensive Security and Performance Assessment of UAV Authentication Schemes
A Review of On-Device Machine Learning for IoT: An Energy Perspective
item.description:
Research overview

This review examines the energy demands of running machine learning close to IoT devices. It organizes research on training and inference, including centralized, distributed, and federated approaches, and discusses the relationship between model performance, resource consumption, privacy, and latency. The survey complements our experimental study of on-device intrusion detection and identifies challenges for energy-efficient deployment.

item.title: Augmenting Security and Privacy in the Virtual Realm: An Analysis of Extended Reality Devices
item.description:
Research overview

This article analyzes security and privacy attacks and defenses from the perspective of extended-reality devices. It examines the risks created by their capabilities and considers how protections can better account for sensitive user information. The analysis develops research directions and design considerations for more secure, privacy-aware XR systems, providing context for our later VR sensor side-channel study.

item.title: EVOKE: Efficient Revocation of Verifiable Credentials in IoT Networks
item.description:
Research overview

EVOKE addresses credential revocation in IoT networks where devices have limited storage, processing power, and connectivity. It uses an elliptic-curve-based accumulator and supports both mass revocation and offline updates. We implemented a prototype and evaluated its storage, latency, and update propagation across deployment scenarios, including commodity IoT devices and hybrid networks.

item.title: Exploring Jamming and Hijacking Attacks for Micro Aerial Drones
item.description:
Research overview

We investigate jamming and hijacking attacks against the Crazy Real Time Protocol used by Crazyflie micro aerial drones. Experiments on a Crazyflie 2.1 examine disruption in autonomous and non-autonomous flight modes. The study connects wireless communication weaknesses with flight reliability and discusses potential defenses and the practical constraints involved in protecting resource-limited aerial devices.

item.title: MacOS versus Microsoft Windows: A Study on the Cybersecurity and Privacy User Perception of Two Popular Operating Systems
item.description:
Research overview

We surveyed 208 macOS and Windows users to examine how they perceive the security and privacy of their operating systems. Many participants viewed macOS as more secure and private, often relying on reputation rather than technical considerations. The study also identifies misconceptions and differences in protective behavior, showing how confidence in a platform can affect the precautions its users take.

item.title: On the Robustness of Image-Based Malware Detection Against Adversarial Attacks
item.description:
Research overview

We evaluate a CNN that classifies image representations of Windows executable files alongside MalConv under four functionality-preserving adversarial attacks. The tested image-based classifier was more resistant to black-box byte-append attacks, while both models remained vulnerable to white-box FGSM attacks. The chapter shows why a detector’s normal classification performance must be assessed separately from its resistance to deliberate evasion.
